hotspots.name: Notice Board
hotspots.examine: A notice board covered in printouts. One catches your eye — a password reminder from 'IT Support'.

hotspots.name: Reception Desk
hotspots.examine: The reception desk. A sign reads: 'All visitors must sign in. Tailgating is a security violation.'

hotspots.name: Security Poster
hotspots.examine: A Government of Canada security awareness poster. It says: 'Think Before You Click. Report Suspicious Emails.'

hotspots.name: Suspicious Briefcase
hotspots.examine: A briefcase with a USB drive sticking out of the pocket. It looks like it was left here deliberately.

hotspots.name: Unknown USB Drive
hotspots.examine: A USB drive sitting on top of a server. Someone may have left it here, or planted it.

hotspots.name: Server Rack
hotspots.examine: A rack of servers humming quietly. The blinking lights make it look alive. No external devices should be connected to these.

hotspots.name: Access Log Terminal
hotspots.examine: A terminal showing the access log. You notice Wanda's badge was scanned in twice this morning — but she didn't sign the physical visitor log.

hotspots.name: Secure Entry Door
hotspots.examine: The secure entry to the building. A badge reader is mounted beside it. Wanda is holding the door open and waving you through.

hotspots.name: Badge Reader
hotspots.examine: The electronic badge reader. All employees must tap their own badge to enter — no exceptions. Piggybacking behind another person is a policy violation.

hotspots.name: Security Sign
hotspots.examine: A posted sign reads: 'ONE PERSON PER BADGE SWIPE. Tailgating is a security violation and may result in disciplinary action. Report incidents to 1-800-GOV-SAFE.'

hotspots.name: Wanda's Laptop
hotspots.examine: Wanda's laptop is open, facing the cafeteria. A spreadsheet is clearly visible showing employee names and salary bands. Anyone walking by can read it.

hotspots.name: Lunch Counter
hotspots.examine: The lunch counter. Today's special: vegetable soup and a bun. Nothing suspicious here — though you can see Wanda's screen from here too.

hotspots.name: Privacy Reminder
hotspots.examine: A Treasury Board of Canada poster: 'Protect Sensitive Information. In public spaces, use a privacy screen and be aware of who can see your work.'

hotspots.name: Unlocked Workstation
hotspots.examine: Justin's government workstation. The screen is unlocked and showing an open email with sensitive departmental figures. Anyone walking by can read it.

hotspots.name: Sticky Note
hotspots.examine: A yellow sticky note stuck to the monitor bezel. It reads: 'Password: Canada2024!' in blue pen. Anyone at the desk can read it.

hotspots.name: Document Pile
hotspots.examine: A pile of printed documents marked PROTECTED B. They're sitting face-up on an unattended desk. The Clean Desk Policy requires these to be locked away when not in active use.

hotspots.name: Unidentified Visitor
hotspots.examine: A person sitting at the boardroom table. She is not wearing a visitor badge, a staff ID, or any visible identification. This is a restricted meeting room.

hotspots.name: Projector Screen
hotspots.examine: The projector is showing a slide deck with a PROTECTED B header. The boardroom has a glass wall facing the main corridor — the content is visible to anyone passing by.

hotspots.name: Whiteboard
hotspots.examine: The whiteboard has names, org chart boxes, and budget figures written in marker. Previous meeting notes — including a staffing decision marked 'CONFIDENTIAL' — were not erased. A clean-whiteboard policy applies to shared meeting rooms.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: There's a notice pinned up here: 'Urgent — Please reset your password by clicking the link below. — IT Support.' Something feels off.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Psst — Justin. Before you do anything, what do you usually check in an email like that?

choices.label: Click the link immediately

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You click the link. A fake login page appears. Your credentials are now compromised. Wanda smiles from across the lobby.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Hmm. What could you have checked before clicking that link?

choices.label: Check the sender's email address first

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I look at the sender: 'it-support@gov-ca-helpdesk.net'. That's not a government domain. That's a red flag.

choices.label: Report it to IT Security without clicking

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I forward the notice details to itsecurity@canada.ca and mark it as suspected phishing.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: That's exactly right. Reporting suspicious communications protects everyone on the network. Well done!

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Good catch. Now that you know it's suspicious — what's the right next step?

choices.label: Delete it and say nothing

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Others might still fall for it. Deleting without reporting leaves the threat active.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: If you spotted a suspicious email, who else in the building might receive the same one?

choices.label: Report it to IT Security

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I report the suspicious notice to IT Security immediately.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Perfect. You stopped potential harm to the whole network.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: What can you do right now to limit the damage from clicking that link?

choices.label: Report it to IT Security and change my password

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I call IT Security right away and change my password from a secure device.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Fast action after an incident matters. You may have limited the exposure.

choices.label: Hope no one notices

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The incident goes unreported. The attacker maintains access for days.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: An unknown USB drive just sitting here on the server. It could be anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: USB drives found in unexpected places are a classic social engineering attack. They may contain malware that auto-runs when inserted.

choices.label: Plug it in to see what's on it

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The moment it's connected, a script runs. The server room lights flicker. Something is spreading across the network.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: What should you have done instead of plugging it in?

choices.label: Leave it alone and report it to Security

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I don't touch it. I photograph it with my phone and call IT Security to report a suspicious device.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Exactly right. Never plug in unknown devices. Report and let trained staff handle it.

choices.label: Pocket it to examine later on a personal device

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your personal device is compromised within seconds of plugging it in.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Unknown devices are dangerous on any machine — personal or government. What's the safe move?

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: The access log shows Wanda's badge scanned twice today — but I saw her in the lobby, not in here. And she didn't sign the physical visitor log.

choices.label: Ignore it — probably a system glitch

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Possible tailgating incidents left uninvestigated are a real insider threat risk.

choices.label: Report the anomaly to the Security Officer

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I flag the access log anomaly to the building Security Officer.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Good. Unusual access patterns are worth reporting. It could be nothing — or it could be tailgating. Either way, it's not your call to ignore it.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Let's think this through. What happens to data on a network when an unknown device is connected?

choices.label: The device could run malware automatically

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: Right. Auto-run scripts, keyloggers, ransomware — a single device can compromise an entire network segment.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Exactly. The correct action is always: don't touch it, photograph it, call IT Security. They have forensic tools to examine it safely.

choices.label: Report it to IT Security immediately

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I call IT Security and report a suspicious device. I don't touch it again.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: That's the right call — even after a mistake. Fast reporting limits the damage and starts the incident response process.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: The briefcase has a USB drive in the pocket. It wasn't there an hour ago.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A USB drive left unattended in a public area of a government building. Wanda has stepped away from her seat.

choices.label: Take the USB drive to examine it

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Hmm. What are the risks of handling unknown devices taken from a stranger's belongings?

choices.label: Report the unattended bag and USB to Security

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I alert building security about an unattended bag with an exposed USB drive.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Correct. Unattended items in secure areas are a physical security concern — not just a technical one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Wanda holds the secure entry door open and waves you through with a smile. The badge reader blinks, waiting for a tap.

lines.speaker: wanda
lines.text: Come on through — don't worry about the reader, I've got it.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Hold on, Justin. What does the policy say about entering through a door held open by someone else?

choices.label: Follow her through without badging

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You follow Wanda through the door. The badge log now shows only one entry for two people. This is a tailgating incident.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: One badge swipe, two people through the door. What could go wrong with that record?

choices.label: Tap your own badge and enter separately

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I step back and tap my own badge before entering. Every person must authenticate individually.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Right. Even if it feels awkward, your badge is your identity on the access log. Never share an entry swipe.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: The badge reader exists so every entry is attributable to an individual. If Wanda was unauthorized, the log now shows nothing. What's the right move now?

choices.label: Report the tailgating incident to Security

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I contact the Security desk to report that I entered without badging and that an unknown person may have accessed the building.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Reporting after the fact is still the right thing to do. Incident response can begin and the log gap can be flagged.

choices.label: Say nothing — it was just Wanda

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The incident goes unreported. The access log has a gap. If something happens later, there is no record.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: 'Just' never makes a security gap smaller — it just makes it undocumented.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: Wanda's laptop is open in the cafeteria. I can clearly see a spreadsheet with employee names and their salary bands.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is Protected B information — restricted to authorized personnel. Displaying it in a public cafeteria violates the Department's information handling policy.

choices.label: Say nothing and keep walking

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The data remains visible to everyone in the cafeteria. Passersby, contractors, and visitors all walk past Wanda's screen.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: What's the risk of leaving sensitive data visible in a shared space — even if you didn't put it there?

choices.label: Politely ask Wanda to angle her screen

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: Excuse me — I can see Protected B data on your screen from here. You might want to angle it away from the aisle.

lines.speaker: wanda
lines.text: Oh — right. Thanks.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Good instinct. Speaking up about visible sensitive data is part of your security responsibility, even for a colleague's screen.

choices.label: Report the data exposure to the Privacy Officer

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I discretely note the incident and contact the departmental Privacy Officer to report that Protected B data was visible in a public cafeteria.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Reporting to the Privacy Officer creates a record and may trigger a broader review. That's exactly the right level of response for a data exposure incident.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Sensitive data visible in a public space is an exposure incident — whether or not anyone malicious saw it. What's the right step now?

choices.label: Move away quietly

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The exposure continues unreported. Without a record, the department cannot improve its training or access controls.

choices.label: Alert the Privacy Officer

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I report the data exposure to the Privacy Officer — better late than never.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Reporting even after the fact starts the incident response process. A late report is far better than no report.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: My workstation is unlocked. An email with departmental budget figures is open on the screen. I've been away from my desk for ten minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The Directive on Security Management requires workstations to be locked when unattended, even for brief absences.

choices.label: Leave it — I'll be back in a minute

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A colleague notices the open screen and reads the budget email without authorization. An unattended workstation is an open invitation.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: How long does it take for unauthorized access to occur on an unlocked, unattended workstation?

choices.label: Lock the screen now (Win+L)

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I lock the screen immediately. No matter how brief the absence, the workstation should always be locked.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Correct. Win+L is a reflex, not an option. An unlocked screen is an unlocked door.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: An unlocked workstation can be accessed by anyone in seconds. What should you do right now to reduce the risk?

choices.label: Lock the screen and set auto-lock to 5 minutes

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I lock the screen immediately, then set the auto-lock timer to 5 minutes as a backup for next time.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Auto-lock is a safety net — not a replacement for locking manually when you leave. But having both is good defence-in-depth.

choices.label: Ignore it and hope nothing happened

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The incident goes unaddressed. The same situation will happen again.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: There's a sticky note on my monitor. It reads: 'Password: Canada2024!' in blue pen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Written passwords are a direct violation of the department's password management policy. Anyone with physical access to the desk can read it — including cleaners, contractors, and visitors.

choices.label: It's fine — nobody will look twice

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A contractor doing repair work in the office reads the sticky note. By end of week, the account is used to access restricted files.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Who has physical access to this desk space over the course of a month?

choices.label: Remove the sticky note and use a password manager

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I remove and shred the sticky note, then log a request to have a departmental password manager installed on my workstation.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: A password manager means you only need to remember one strong passphrase. No sticky notes, no repeated passwords, no guessable patterns.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: A written password is accessible to anyone with eyes and physical proximity. What's the immediate fix?

choices.label: Remove the note and report to IT for a password manager

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I shred the sticky note and submit an IT request for a password manager. I also change the exposed password immediately.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Change the password first — that limits the exposure window. Then request the password manager so it doesn't happen again.

choices.label: Just remove the note

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Better than nothing. But the password that was written down should also be changed — it may already have been seen.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: There's a person at the boardroom table with no visible visitor badge, no staff ID, and no escort. The meeting is about to begin.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Visitor policy requires all non-staff to be issued a visitor badge at reception and escorted at all times within the secure zone.

choices.label: Assume someone else checked her in

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The meeting proceeds. Later, it emerges that the visitor was never signed in and had no authorization to attend the briefing.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: If not you, then who? What happens when everyone in the room makes that same assumption?

choices.label: Politely ask to see her visitor badge

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: Excuse me — I don't see a visitor badge. Could you show me your ID or have reception confirm your access?

lines.speaker: wanda
lines.text: I... left it at the front desk. I'll go get it.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: A calm, professional challenge is not rude — it is exactly what the policy asks of every employee.

choices.label: Report an unescorted visitor to Security

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I step into the corridor and call Security to report an unidentified person in the secure boardroom without visible credentials.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Reporting rather than confronting directly is often the safer choice. Security can verify identity without creating a confrontational scene.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: An unverified person has now attended a protected briefing. What's the right move to limit the damage?

choices.label: Report the incident to Security after the meeting

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I report to Security that an unverified individual attended the briefing without visible credentials. I provide a description.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Late reporting still triggers an investigation. It may also prompt a security review of the meeting's content to assess what was disclosed.

choices.label: Say nothing — the meeting is over

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The incident is unreported. The unauthorized attendee leaves the building unchallenged with whatever they heard in the briefing.

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: The projector is displaying a PROTECTED B slide deck. The boardroom has a glass wall facing the main corridor — anyone walking by can see the screen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Displaying classified or protected information where unauthorized persons can view it is an information security incident, regardless of intent.

choices.label: Continue the meeting — it's probably fine

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Three people walk past the glass wall during the presentation and can read the protected slide content.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: What's the difference between accidental disclosure and intentional disclosure in terms of the impact on the department?

choices.label: Close the corridor blinds and reposition the screen

lines.speaker: justin
lines.text: I close the blinds on the corridor-facing wall and ask if the screen can be angled away from the glass before we continue.

lines.speaker: smarty
lines.text: Good. Before displaying protected information, always assess who else can see the screen — including outside the room.

reporter.name: First Responder
reporter.desc: Reported a suspicious communication or device to IT Security.

usb_aware.name: USB Aware
usb_aware.desc: Refused to plug in an unknown USB device and reported it.

vigilant.name: Vigilant
vigilant.desc: Noticed and reported an access log anomaly.

quick_recovery.name: Quick Recovery
quick_recovery.desc: Reported a phishing incident and changed credentials promptly after clicking a bad link.

data_guardian.name: Data Guardian
data_guardian.desc: Completed all modules without accumulating a risk score above 20.

door_guardian.name: Door Guardian
door_guardian.desc: Refused to tailgate through a secure entry and badged in properly.

screen_guardian.name: Screen Guardian
screen_guardian.desc: Spoke up about sensitive data visible on an unattended or public-facing screen.

clean_desk.name: Clean Desk
clean_desk.desc: Secured an unlocked workstation or removed a written password from view.

access_control.name: Access Control
access_control.desc: Challenged or reported an unescorted visitor in a restricted area.
